newsitem.title: CHINA: South China has much to thank Deng Xiaoping.
newsitem.headline: South China has much to thank Deng Xiaoping.

text.p: China's southern provinces of Guangdong and Fujian owe much to Deng Xiaoping.

For the first 30 years of Communist Party rule after 1949, the two basically agricultural provinces, among China's poorest, had to languish while Beijing chose to invest in the northeast and in the interior.

But after Deng took over in 1978 he used Guangdong as a cradle for economic reform, giving it preferential tax policies to attract investment from neighbouring Hong Kong, and allowing it to retain most of its tax revenues.
He later extended the same privileges to Fujian, opposite Taiwan, to attract investors from the breakaway island.
The results were dramatic.
Guangdong's Gross Domestic Product in 1994 was 417.5 billion yuan ($50.3 billion), ranking first among all cities and provinces in China, more than 10 times the pre-1978 figure.
In 1994, its foreign trade was $96.66 billion, accounting for 41 percent of China's total, and attracted $9.4 billion in actual foreign investment, 28 percent of the national total.
Guangdong has three of China's four Special Economic Zones -- brainchilds of Deng's reform process -- and one of its two stock markets.

In 1994, Fujian's GDP reached 145 billion yuan ($17.5 billion), six times the 1978 figure. Its foreign trade in 1994 was $12.86 billion, ranking fourth in the nation, with $4 billion in actual foreign investment.
This spectacular growth has been largely outside the state sector -- in foreign-invested, private and collective firms, all banned in pre-1978 China.

Many of the new factories were export-oriented, processing imported or local materials to sell to foreign markets, moved by their owners from Hong Kong and Taiwan to make use of the much lower wages in mainland China.
"Deng's success was to tap the enormous economic potential of Hong Kong and later Taiwan that were looking for cheaper places to manufacture their goods," a Chinese economist said.
"What he gave Guangdong and Fujian was not money but policies, in investment and tax, so that they would develop under their own steam, without money from Beijing," he said.
Guangdong and Fujian would not enjoy their present prosperity without Deng, said Zhang Xianyang, a researcher with the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences.
"It was he who saw that China had to use capital from abroad and that investors from Hong Kong were the best potential providers," he said.
"It was Deng who protected the two provinces in the 1980s from conservatives in the leadership who opposed the preferential policies given to them," he said.
In early 1992, after many in Beijing had criticised the special economic zones as the return of capitalism, Deng defied poor health to tour Guangdong where he voiced support for both provinces.
His visit, known as the "southern tour", sparked rapid economic growth nationwide.

The political result of this astonishing growth is that Guangdong has become increasingly self-reliant for capital, giving Beijing less and less leverage over it, allowing it to finance ambitious projects such as a subway and expressways.
It has also produced unwelcome side-effects, such as prostitution, drug-taking and gambling as well as gangs who control much of this trade.
Commenting on the future for Guangdong and Fujian, Zhang said: "One generation can only achieve one thing. Our grandsons can work to achieve justice and fairness."

In the China of the late chairman Mao Zedong, the two provinces suffered from their proximity to Taiwan, seat of the Nationalist leader Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek, defeated by Mao in China's civil war but who vowed to reconquer the mainland.

Mao, fearing a U.S.-backed invasion by Chiang, ruled that the two provinces were on the front line and not suitable for large-scale investment. Deng oversaw resumption of ties with the United States and a tentative warming of ties with Taiwan that paved the way for the boom and the fastest economic growth on earth in Guangdong and Fujian.
